How to use this workbook

  1. Review the transition appendix before beginning. It contains every transition blanked anywhere in the workbook.
  2. Read the complete context before filling any blank. Identify the relationship first: addition, contrast, concession, cause, result, example, sequence, condition, clarification, or conclusion.
  3. Type the transition directly into each inline box. You must also insert any necessary comma yourself. Periods and semicolons are already shown.
  4. Open the jumbled hint only when needed. The hint contains the original transition words without commas and in a different order whenever the item contains more than one distinguishable answer.
  5. Open “Possible answers” after completing the item. More than one answer may work; compare meaning, grammar, naturalness, register, and punctuation.
  6. For personalised feedback, open the GPT prompt. It automatically includes the task, blanked text, and your current answers. Copy it into ChatGPT without changing it.
REMEMBER

A transition is not correct merely because it is grammatically possible. It must express the exact relationship between the ideas and sound appropriate for the task. Spoken answers normally use simpler, more conversational transitions than formal writing.

CHAPTER

Part 1 · Short Contexts

Begin with focused paragraphs and sentence groups. Each item contains only one to three blanks, so you can practise identifying one logical relationship at a time.

Original exercise set

ITEM 1

Short Context 1

Mina studied carefully for the examination. [1.1] she still felt nervous when she entered the classroom.
Hint: jumbled transition bank
Nevertheless

Commas are not shown in the hint. Add them where the sentence requires them.

Possible answers
[1.1]
Original: Nevertheless,
Other natural possibilities: Nonetheless, • Even so, • Still, • However, • Despite this, • In spite of this,

These lists contain the natural standard answers supported by the context. Because language is open-ended, another carefully justified answer may occasionally work.

[1.3] the other volunteers could move quickly across open sand, we had to climb carefully between slippery stones. ITEM 2

Urban Trees and Heat

Cities are often warmer than surrounding rural areas because roads, roofs, and other built surfaces absorb solar energy during the day and release it slowly at night. This pattern is known as the urban heat island effect; [2.1] neighbourhoods with limited vegetation may remain several degrees warmer than nearby parks. The difference matters because prolonged heat increases the risk of dehydration, heart problems, and heat-related death, especially among older adults and people without air conditioning.

Urban trees can reduce these temperatures in two main ways. Their leaves block sunlight from reaching pavement and building walls. [2.2] water released through their leaves cools the surrounding air through a process called transpiration. A mature tree can therefore create a noticeably cooler area beneath its canopy. [2.3] a single tree cannot change the temperature of an entire district. Significant cooling usually requires a connected network of trees, shrubs, and other green spaces.

Researchers must consider more than the number of trees when evaluating such programmes. Tree species differ in canopy size, water needs, growth rate, and tolerance for pollution. [2.4] a fast-growing species may provide shade quickly but become vulnerable during drought. A slower-growing native tree may survive longer and support local wildlife; [2.5] it may take many years to produce a broad canopy. Planting location is equally important. Trees placed beside west-facing walls can reduce afternoon heat indoors; [2.6] trees planted beneath power lines may require repeated cutting and never reach their full size.

Access also affects the success of urban forestry. Wealthier areas often have older, larger trees, [2.7] low-income neighbourhoods may contain fewer shaded streets despite facing greater heat exposure. Cities can address this imbalance by prioritising the hottest districts and consulting residents before planting begins. Community involvement improves maintenance [2.8] residents are more likely to water and protect trees they helped select.

Urban trees are not a complete solution to extreme heat; [2.9] they can form an important part of a broader strategy that includes reflective roofs, shaded bus stops, efficient buildings, and public cooling centres. When these measures are planned together, cities become cooler, healthier, and more resilient. [2.10] urban forestry should be treated not as decoration but as essential infrastructure.

For a moment, she could not understand what had happened. [3.4] the image of the case beside the station bench returned to her mind. Mara jumped up and found the conductor. She explained that the violin belonged to her school and that she needed it for an audition the following morning. [3.5] the conductor could not stop the express train between stations. He contacted Central Station by radio and asked the staff to search platform six.

The next twenty minutes seemed longer than the entire journey. Mara imagined the case being stolen, damaged, or sent to a distant lost-property office. [3.6] the conductor returned with encouraging news: a cleaner had found it. The station manager would keep it locked away until Mara returned.

She got off at the next stop and waited for the train going back. [3.7] she called her teacher and admitted what she had done. She expected anger; [3.8] her teacher laughed and said that every musician eventually learned to guard an instrument more carefully than a wallet.

Mara recovered the violin shortly before sunset; [3.9] she missed the last rehearsal in Northbridge. The audition still took place the next morning. [3.10] she played with unusual concentration because she understood how close she had come to losing the chance. She did not win first prize; [3.11] she received a special mention for musical expression. From that day forward, the violin case never left her hand in a station.

ITEM 4

The Printing Press and the Spread of Ideas

Before mechanical printing became common in Europe, books were copied by hand. Monks, professional scribes, and university workers could spend months reproducing a single manuscript; [4.1] books were expensive and relatively rare. Libraries protected their collections carefully, and many ordinary people never owned a book. Knowledge still travelled through letters, lectures, sermons, and handwritten copies; [4.2] the speed and scale of that movement remained limited.

In the mid-fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg developed a practical system that combined movable metal type, oil-based ink, a press, and methods for producing many identical letters. He did not invent every part of the process; [4.3] his achievement was to combine existing techniques into an efficient system. Printers could rearrange reusable pieces of type to create new pages; [4.4] they no longer needed to carve an entire page into a single wooden block.

The new technology reduced the time required to reproduce a text; [4.5] it gradually lowered the cost of books. Early printed works were still valuable objects, and many were decorated by hand; [4.6] production increased dramatically compared with manuscript copying. Printing shops appeared in major European cities, often near universities, courts, and trade centres. Religious texts remained important; [4.7] printers also produced calendars, scientific works, political arguments, maps, and practical manuals.

The printing press did not automatically create widespread literacy. Many people could not read, and books were still beyond the reach of the poorest families; [4.8] printed material became more available to merchants, students, officials, and skilled workers. Readers could compare multiple copies of the same text, and scholars could respond to one another across long distances; [4.9] debates developed more rapidly and reached larger audiences.

The technology also created new problems. Errors could be reproduced hundreds of times, and authorities worried about criticism spreading beyond their control; [4.10] governments and religious institutions introduced licences, censorship, and punishments for printers. Such restrictions sometimes slowed publication; [4.11] they could not fully reverse the growth of print culture.

Mechanical printing transformed communication over several centuries rather than overnight; [4.12] its long-term effect was profound. By making identical texts easier to produce and circulate, the press helped reshape education, religion, science, commerce, and political life.

ITEM 5

Why Secondary Schools Should Start Later

Many secondary schools begin classes before eight in the morning. This schedule may be convenient for transport systems, sports programmes, and parents’ working hours; [5.1] it often conflicts with adolescent sleep patterns. Teenagers tend to fall asleep later than younger children, partly because of biological changes; [5.2] asking them to wake at five or six o’clock can leave them chronically tired even when they try to maintain responsible routines.

Supporters of early schedules argue that students should simply go to bed sooner. [5.3] this advice ignores the fact that sleep timing is not controlled by discipline alone. Homework, family responsibilities, part-time jobs, and evening activities can also delay bedtime. A student who reaches home after practice at seven, eats dinner, and completes several assignments may not be able to sleep at nine. [5.4] an early start can punish students for demands created by the school itself.

Later start times may improve more than alertness. Well-rested students are more likely to concentrate, participate, and regulate their emotions; [5.5] teachers may spend less time repeating instructions or managing behaviour caused by exhaustion. Attendance may improve as well, because fewer students oversleep or miss the first lesson. [5.6] schools that begin later may see academic and social benefits at the same time.

Changing the timetable is not effortless. Bus routes may need to be redesigned, sports practices may end later, and families with younger children may face coordination problems; [5.7] these challenges are logistical rather than educational. Communities routinely adjust schedules when a policy is important enough. [5.8] schools could introduce the change gradually, coordinate with local transport providers, and offer supervised morning spaces for students who must arrive early.

A later start is not a cure for every problem. Students may still use phones late at night, and heavy workloads can continue to reduce sleep; [5.9] a more suitable timetable removes one major obstacle that schools directly control. Education depends on students being mentally present; [5.10] requiring them to learn while biologically unprepared to be awake is counterproductive. Secondary schools should therefore treat sleep as a condition for learning, not as a private matter unrelated to academic policy.

ITEM 7

The Engineer Who Listened First

When agricultural engineer Laila Mensah first visited the farming community of Nembasa, she expected to recommend a modern irrigation pump. The region experienced long dry seasons, and many fields depended on water carried by hand from shallow wells; [7.1] Laila assumed that a solar-powered system would immediately solve the problem. During her first meetings, however, the farmers asked questions she had not considered: Who would repair the pump? Could replacement parts be purchased locally? Would every family receive equal access to the water?

Laila postponed her original proposal and spent six weeks observing daily routines. She learned that several earlier development projects had failed after outside specialists left; [7.2] equipment had broken, instructions had been written in unfamiliar technical language, and no local repair fund had been created. The technology itself had sometimes worked well; [7.3] the surrounding plan had not.

She returned to her university and redesigned the project with a smaller team. The new pump used common parts available in the nearest town; [7.4] it produced less water than the original model. Its lower capacity appeared to be a disadvantage; [7.5] it made the system cheaper, easier to repair, and suitable for the existing well. The farmers also formed a committee to schedule water use and collect small maintenance payments.

Installation began at the start of the next dry season. Laila trained three residents to inspect the panels, replace worn components, and record the pump’s performance; [7.6] she asked them to modify the training materials whenever an explanation seemed unclear. The final manual contained diagrams, local terms, and photographs taken during installation.

The pump did not transform Nembasa overnight. Crop yields increased gradually, and some families continued carrying water when demand was high; [7.7] the system remained operational for five years without requiring an outside technician. Nearby communities began requesting similar projects; [7.8] Laila refused to copy the design without first studying each location.

Her later work followed the same principle: engineering begins with careful listening. [7.9] technical knowledge is essential, but it cannot replace local knowledge. ITEM 8

How a Damaged Wetland Can Be Restored

Wetlands filter water, reduce flooding, store carbon, and provide habitat for many species. They can be damaged when rivers are redirected, land is drained, invasive plants spread, or roads interrupt the natural movement of water; [8.1] restoration begins with understanding what changed and why. Workers cannot simply add water or plant reeds and assume that the original ecosystem will return.

The first stage is investigation. Ecologists map the site, test the soil, measure water levels, and compare present conditions with historical records. [8.2] they may interview nearby residents who remember earlier flooding patterns or wildlife populations. This information helps the team identify the main causes of decline. [8.3] a wetland that dried because of a blocked stream requires a different response from one contaminated by industrial waste.

The next priority is usually water flow. Engineers may remove drainage pipes, lower artificial barriers, or reconnect an old river channel; [8.4] changes must be introduced carefully. Restoring too much water too quickly can flood neighbouring property or wash away unstable soil. Teams often begin with a small section and monitor the results. [8.5] successful adjustments can then be expanded.

Plant recovery may occur naturally once suitable water conditions return; [8.6] native species sometimes need to be replanted, especially where invasive plants dominate. Restoration workers remove aggressive species and introduce plants adapted to different depths and seasons. They may protect new growth from grazing animals; [8.7] young plants can establish strong root systems.

Monitoring continues long after construction ends. Scientists track water quality, plant coverage, bird activity, insects, fish, and soil conditions; [8.8] one positive indicator does not prove that the whole wetland is healthy. An increase in birds may seem encouraging; [8.9] water tests could still reveal pollution or low oxygen levels.

Wetland restoration is therefore an adaptive process rather than a single event. Teams act, measure the results, and revise their methods. [8.10] recovery may take years, and the final ecosystem may not exactly match the historical one. A restored wetland can still perform valuable ecological functions; [8.11] long-term success depends on continued protection from the pressures that caused the original damage.

ITEM 9

A Mountain Town After the Crowds Leave

Most visitors arrive in Bellhaven during the summer festival, when musicians perform in the square and every guesthouse displays a “full” sign. By late October, the banners have been removed, the tour buses have disappeared, and the mountain air has turned sharp; [9.1] the town may seem closed for the season. In reality, autumn reveals a quieter version of Bellhaven that hurried summer visitors rarely notice.

The main street is nearly empty before nine in the morning; [9.2] the bakery beside the clock tower is already busy. Residents stop for dark bread, apple pastries, and coffee before work. Travellers can sit by the window and watch shopkeepers raise their shutters one by one; [9.3] there is no need to compete for a table or rush through breakfast.

Walking trails remain open unless early snow reaches the higher slopes. The route to Lake Orin is especially attractive because yellow leaves cover the lower forest; [9.4] the path can become muddy after rain, so waterproof shoes are essential. The lake itself is colder and less colourful than it appears in summer photographs; [9.5] its still surface and empty shoreline create a different kind of beauty.

Some seasonal attractions do close. Boat rentals end in September, and the hilltop café operates only at weekends; [9.6] museums, craft workshops, and family-run restaurants continue throughout the year. Visitors who ask about opening hours in advance can still fill several days without difficulty. Prices are often lower as well; [9.7] many hotels offer weekday discounts once the festival period ends.

Evenings require a slower rhythm. There are few late-night venues, and streets become silent soon after dinner; [9.8] travellers expecting constant entertainment may feel restless. Those willing to read, talk with local residents, or simply rest may appreciate the calm.

Bellhaven in autumn is not a substitute for Bellhaven in summer; [9.9] it is a distinct experience. The season exchanges performances and crowds for open paths, unhurried conversations, and a closer view of daily life; [9.10] visitors should come prepared for uncertain weather and limited schedules. With those expectations, the town’s quietest months can also be its most memorable.

ITEM 10

Reducing Food Waste in University Cafeterias

University cafeterias prepare thousands of meals each week, and some waste is difficult to avoid. Demand changes from day to day, ingredients expire, and students sometimes leave food uneaten; [10.1] the amount discarded is not fixed or inevitable. Better information, flexible serving systems, and clearer communication can reduce waste without limiting students’ choices.

The first problem is inaccurate forecasting. Cafeterias may prepare the same quantity every Tuesday even when attendance varies because of exams, holidays, or campus events; [10.2] managers should compare sales records with the academic calendar and update estimates regularly. Advance meal reservations can provide additional information; [10.3] reservations should guide production rather than become a strict requirement that excludes spontaneous customers.

Portion size is another major source of waste. A standard serving may be too large for some students and too small for others; [10.4] offering two portion sizes allows people to choose more realistically. Self-service stations can also help; [10.5] they must be monitored to prevent students from taking excessive amounts simply because food appears unlimited. Signs can encourage diners to begin with a small serving and return for more if necessary.

Communication matters as much as measurement. Students may reject a dish because its ingredients or level of spiciness are unclear; [10.6] accurate labels can reduce unwanted selections. Cafeterias can also display the amount of food wasted each day; [10.7] visible data turns an abstract environmental issue into a shared campus problem. Campaigns should avoid blaming individual students [10.8] the institution also controls purchasing, menu design, storage, and serving practices.

Some surplus food can be donated when safety rules permit; [10.9] donation should not replace prevention. Producing too much food and then giving part of it away still consumes energy, water, labour, and money. Unavoidable scraps can be composted; [10.10] edible food should remain the main target for reduction.

No single measure will eliminate cafeteria waste; [10.11] a coordinated system can produce meaningful results. Universities should forecast demand carefully, offer flexible portions, improve labels, involve students, and track outcomes over time. [10.12] food-waste reduction becomes part of daily management rather than a temporary awareness campaign.

ITEM 11

The Repair Café

On the first Saturday of every month, residents bring broken lamps, radios, bicycles, and small appliances to a community hall. The event is called a repair café. [11.1] the name suggests a commercial service, nobody is charged for the repairs. Volunteers instead teach owners how to identify problems and, when possible, fix the items themselves.

The approach has environmental benefits. A loose wire or worn seal can make an appliance appear useless; [11.2] a simple repair may extend its life for several years. [11.3] the event reduces waste, it helps residents avoid the cost of replacing items unnecessarily. The volunteers do not promise that every object can be saved. [11.4] they examine each item carefully and explain why a repair is safe or unsafe.

The social effects are equally important. People who might never otherwise meet work side by side at long tables. Experienced volunteers share technical knowledge; [11.5] younger participants often help them use digital manuals or order parts online. The exchange is [11.6] practical [11.7] social.

Some manufacturers make repair difficult by sealing devices or refusing to sell replacement parts. [11.8] the café has begun recording which products are easiest to maintain. It publishes the results so residents can consider repairability before buying. [11.9] one local shop now offers a discount on products whose parts can be replaced individually.

The repair café cannot solve the global waste problem by itself. [11.10] it changes how participants think about ownership. A broken object is no longer automatically treated as rubbish. [11.11] it becomes a question: can this be understood, repaired, and used again?

ITEM 12

Why Scientific Replication Matters

A single scientific study can produce an exciting result. [12.1] the methods are careful and the statistics appear strong, the finding may still have occurred by chance. Replication—repeating a study with new participants or data—helps researchers determine whether the original pattern is reliable.

Replication is not simply mechanical repetition. Researchers may use the same procedure to test whether the result appears again; [12.2] they may change the setting or population to see how broadly the conclusion applies. The two approaches answer different questions. [12.3] both strengthen understanding when their methods are transparent.

Failed replications are sometimes described as attacks on the original researchers. [12.4] they are a normal part of science. A result may disappear because the first sample was small, because an unnoticed condition mattered, or because the later study used a different procedure. [12.5] disagreement between studies can reveal which factors deserve closer attention.

Replication can be difficult to fund. New discoveries attract publicity, [12.6] repeating old work may appear less creative. [12.7] journals have historically preferred surprising positive results. This creates a problem: findings may influence policy or medical practice before anyone has checked whether they can be reproduced.

Scientific knowledge should therefore be treated as cumulative rather than final. [12.8] one study supports a conclusion, confidence should increase only when other evidence points in the same direction. [12.9] replication does not weaken science; it is one of the processes that makes science dependable.

ITEM 1

Professor

Others argue that students already have demanding schedules and should be free to choose whether they need such a course. Should personal finance be a required university subject? Why or why not?

Student 1

Emily: I think a personal finance course should be required. Students often begin managing rent, loans, and credit cards for the first time during university. A practical course could help them avoid serious financial mistakes.

Student 2

Marcus: I do not think the course should be mandatory. Students have different needs, and some may already understand these topics. Universities could offer optional workshops instead of adding another graduation requirement.

I agree with Emily that personal finance should be required because financial decisions can affect students for many years. [1.1] a student who misunderstands loan interest may borrow more money than necessary without realizing the long-term cost.

[1.2] optional workshops may mainly attract students who are already interested in financial planning. Students who need the information most may not recognize that need until they have made an expensive mistake.

The course would not have to occupy an entire semester. [1.3] universities could offer a short practical course covering budgeting, credit, taxes, insurance, and student loans.

Some students may already know these subjects; [1.4] they could still benefit from learning how financial rules apply in the country or region where they study.

[1.5] a brief required course would provide useful protection without placing an unreasonable burden on students.

ITEM 2

Fixed Routines and Productivity

PROMPT

Course: Psychology

Professor

People use different strategies to remain productive. Some prefer following a fixed daily routine because predictable schedules reduce distraction and make it easier to develop good habits. Others prefer flexible schedules because they can adjust their work according to their energy, responsibilities, and changing circumstances. Which approach is generally more effective for maintaining productivity?

Student 1

Nina: Fixed routines are more effective because they reduce the number of decisions people must make. When work, exercise, and rest occur at regular times, productive behavior becomes automatic.

Student 2

Daniel: Flexible schedules are better because every day is different. People may have unexpected responsibilities or feel more energetic at different times, so strict routines can become stressful.

I believe a basic routine is useful, although it should contain some flexibility. [2.1] fixed starting times can prevent people from repeatedly delaying difficult tasks.

[2.2] a completely rigid schedule may fail when someone becomes ill, receives an urgent assignment, or must help a family member. Missing one planned activity can then make the entire day feel unsuccessful.

A better approach is to distinguish between fixed priorities and adjustable details. [2.3] a person might always complete two hours of focused work before noon but decide each morning whether to begin at eight or nine.

This method preserves the psychological benefits Nina mentions. [2.4] it also addresses Daniel’s concern that unexpected events require adaptation.

[2.5] productivity depends less on following every minute of a schedule than on consistently protecting time for important activities.

[5.4] the authentic remains would stay protected, while visitors could still gain a clearer impression of the site’s historical appearance. Digital models can also be revised when new evidence is discovered.

[5.5] historical interpretation should be made vivid, but it should not be presented as more certain than the evidence allows.

COVERAGE NOTE

The workbook was audited against common transition categories used by university writing centres: causation, chronology, addition, contrast, example, similarity, clarification, concession, importance, purpose, summary, and conclusion. The additional exercises strengthen forms such as although, even though, despite, even so, nonetheless, nevertheless, yet, moreover, furthermore, not only … but also, and consequently.
